period.label: Remain in Light era / Afrofunk synthesis

position_in_era.primary_genre_lineage: art-rock/new wave channeling Fela Kuti Afrobeat polyrhythm through a funk-adjacent grid
position_in_era.geographic_locus: Compass Point Studios, Nassau, Bahamas; Sigma Sound Studios, Philadelphia
position_in_era.historical_role: David Byrne and Brian Eno used Fela Kuti's Afrodisiac (1973) as a template and built Remain in Light from layered drum-loop jams rather than composed songs, arriving at the same funk-polyrhythm territory as Miss You through an intellectual, studio-as-instrument path that prioritized communal African music-making over rock-band hierarchy.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recording started at Compass Point Studios in July 1980. Rather than writing songs around Byrne's lyrics in advance, the band jammed on looping grooves that Eno then layered with overdubs -- a method Byrne described as sharing 'that ecstatic communal feeling' of African music even when the results did not sound overtly African.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Fela Kuti's Afrodisiac became the explicit template for the album; the band and Eno studied the communal, polyrhythmic structure of Afrobeat in which individual parts interlock rather than accompany a lead. This was a deliberate intellectual counterpoint to the straightforward disco-rock merger represented by Miss You.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: The approach generated internal friction: the album was later noted to have 'silenced their harshest critics, even within the band,' implying that some members were skeptical of the departure from conventional songwriting structure.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Remain in Light was named the best album of 1980 by both Sounds and Melody Maker, and appeared on The New York Times' ten-best list for the year.
